what_it_does: Go is a programming language that lets programs run many lightweight tasks (called goroutines) simultaneously, which communicate by passing messages through channels — think of channels as pipes connecting tasks. A partial deadlock happens when some of those tasks get stuck forever waiting for a message that will never arrive, causing the program to leak memory over time without fully crashing. This paper describes GOLF, a system that piggybacks on Go's existing garbage collector (the built-in mechanism that reclaims unused memory) to detect these stuck tasks: if a goroutine is waiting on a channel that nothing alive can ever send on, it is flagged as dead. Crucially, GOLF then automatically cancels those stuck goroutines and frees their memory, restoring normal operation — something prior tools could not do without stopping the whole program. The detection adds very little time to the regular garbage-collection pause.
